title: AI Agents Revision Notes: Loops, Memory, Multi-Agent and Cost
summary: Quick revision notes on how agents work. They cover the ReAct loop, planning, short-term and long-term memory, multi-agent patterns, stopping conditions, and cost and latency control.

chapters.title: The ReAct Loop Mental Model
points: Agent = LLM + tools + loop. The model picks the next action, code executes it, and the result goes back into the context.
ReAct cycle: Thought (reason about the next step) → Action (tool call with arguments) → Observation (tool result) → repeat until a final answer.
ReAct vs plain chain-of-thought: CoT reasons only from the prompt and cannot fetch facts, while ReAct grounds each step in real tool observations and so hallucinates less.
Example: 'Weather in the capital of France?' → Thought: need capital → search('capital of France') → Observation: Paris → get_weather('Paris') → final answer.
Interview Point: What is the difference between a workflow and an agent? Why does ReAct reduce hallucination compared with CoT alone? What does one loop iteration consist of?

chapters.title: Planning Patterns
points: Plan-and-execute: a planner LLM writes the full step list up front and an executor runs each step. Good for long, predictable tasks.
Re-planning: after each step or failure, check the plan against the observations and revise it. Static plans break when a tool result surprises you.
ReAct vs plan-and-execute: ReAct decides one step at a time, so it is flexible but myopic and costs more calls. Plan-and-execute is cheaper and more coherent but rigid.
Reflection loop: the model critiques its own output and retries (draft → critique → revise). Cap it at 1-3 rounds.
Interview Point: When would you choose plan-and-execute over ReAct? How do you handle a plan that stops matching reality? What does reflection add, and what does it cost?

chapters.title: Short-term vs Long-term Memory
points: Short-term memory = the context window: the current messages, tool calls and results. It is limited in size and lost when the session ends.
Long-term memory = an external store (vector DB, key-value store, files) that persists across sessions and is retrieved by similarity or key lookup.
Keeping short-term memory within budget: sliding window of recent turns, summarize old turns, or trim bulky tool outputs.
Write policy for long-term memory: store only distilled facts (preferences, decisions, outcomes), not raw transcripts. Retrieve top-k relevant items and inject them into the prompt.

Interview Point: How do short-term and long-term memory differ in storage and lifetime? What do you do when the context window fills up? What should you write to long-term memory, and how is it retrieved?

chapters.title: Multi-Agent Patterns
points: Orchestrator-worker (supervisor): one lead agent splits the task, delegates to specialist workers, and merges their results. This is the most common pattern.
Pipeline / handoff: agents run in sequence, with each one passing its output or control to the next (researcher → writer → reviewer).
Debate / critic: separate agents propose and critique, or vote, to improve quality on hard or high-stakes answers.
Single vs multi-agent: use multi-agent only when subtasks are parallel, need separate contexts, or need different tools or prompts. It multiplies token cost and adds coordination failures.
Interview Point: When is a single agent enough? How does an orchestrator-worker setup share context and results? What failures are specific to multi-agent systems?

chapters.title: Stopping Conditions, Cost and Latency
points: Stop signals: the model emits a final answer (no tool call), a max-iterations cap is hit, a token or time budget is exhausted, or a human or guardrail interrupts.
Loop failure: an agent that repeats the same tool call with the same arguments will never converge. Detect repeats, then break out or force a different strategy.
Cost grows with iterations because every step re-sends the whole context. Mitigations: prompt caching, a smaller model for easy steps, trimmed tool outputs, and a hard step cap.
Latency levers: run independent tool calls in parallel, stream output, cut the number of steps, and route simple requests to a fast model.
Interview Point: How do you guarantee an agent terminates? Why does cost grow faster than linearly with steps? What would you do to cut latency without losing quality?

chapters.title: Agents Cheat Sheet
points: Loop: Thought → Action → Observation → repeat. Stop on a final answer, a step cap, a budget limit, or a guardrail.
Planning: ReAct for adaptive tasks, plan-and-execute for long predictable tasks, re-plan on surprises, and reflect 1-3 rounds at most.
Memory: short-term is the context window (window, summarize or trim it). Long-term is an external store that holds distilled facts and is retrieved top-k.
Multi-agent and cost: orchestrator-worker by default, start with a single agent, and control cost with a step cap, prompt caching, a small model for easy steps, and parallel tool calls.
Interview Point: Summarize the agent loop in one sentence. Which three limits do you always put on a production agent? How do you pick between single and multi-agent?
